meaning: (1) the son of Alice; (2) the son of Alice, from the popular dim. Alison; (3) the son of Allen, corrupted from Allenson
author_comment: (2) cf. Marion from Mary, Gibbon from Gib (i.e. Gilbert), Beaton from Beatrice, &c. (3) Such a corruption was bound to take place; cf. Pattinson and Pattison. There can be no doubt many of our Allisons are traceable to this source. For early instances, v. Allenson. Allison has ramified very strongly in the United States.

meaning: variant of Albutt
(1) the son of Alcuin (v. Yonge, ii. 350), corrupted to Oldcorn in north England; (2) of Alchorne, a manor in the parish of Rotherfield, co. Sussex, where the family lived in the 14th century
author_comment: I have one representative in my parish (Ulverston). I place all these surnames together because it is impossible to separate them. No doubt both (2) and (1) have assimilated. In a general way Alchorn represents the local, and Alcorn the personal surname. (2) Some of their descendants, still resident in that parish, have, within a generation or two, corrupted their name to Allcorn (Lower).
source: Hundred Rolls, 1273
record_text: Richard Halchein, co. Oxf., 1273. A.

meaning: the son of Aldy, a popular form of Aldwin, or Aldred, or Aldrich, or Aldus, or some other of the once popular compounds of Ald
author_comment: But the probable ancestor was Aldwin, which was early modified into Aldwy; v. Allvey.
